items.title: Headlines for October 27, 2026 | Democracy Now!
items.excerpt: ## Netanyahu Battles to Hold Power as Israel Holds First Election in Four Years Oct 27, 2026 Voters in Israel are heading to the polls today in the first general election in nearly four years. At stake are 120 seats in Israel’s parliament, the Knesset, where 61 votes will be needed to form a majority. Likud party leader Benjamin Netanyahu is seeking to extend his term as Israel’s longest-serving prime minister — that’s despite a warrant issued by the International Criminal Court seeking his arrest for war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Gaza. Netanyahu also faces criminal charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust. His main challenger is Israel’s former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, who supports illegal Israeli settlements, opposes a Palestinian state and has vowed to destroy Hamas’s military wing in Gaza within 18 months. A prominent Palestinian citizen of Israel, Sami Abu Shehadeh, who leads the Palestinian nationalist political party Balad, was forced out of the race. Meanwhile, millions of Palestinians living under Israeli occupation in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza Strip are ineligible to vote — even as election officials set up polling stations in illegal Israeli settlements. ## U.N. Commission of Inquiry Finds Israel Committed Genocide in Gaza, War Crimes in West Bank Oct 27, 2026 A United Nations commission of inquiry has accused Israel of committing genocide in the Gaza Strip during the war that followed the October 7, 2023, attacks. The report published Monday by the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory found Israel’s attacks on Gaza were intended to “destroy the Palestinian people, in whole or in part.” The commission also accused Israel of committing crimes against humanity in the occupied West Bank, including extermination, torture and rape. The report was released as Israeli attacks on Gaza killed at least five Palestinians, including a 7-year-old girl. Meanwhile, in the occupied West Bank, Israeli forces have continued a large-scale offensive for a fifth consecutive day in the city of Hebron, where officials say nearly 5,000 Palestinians have been forced from their homes. ## Humanitarian Crisis Grows as Houthis Lay Siege to Yemen’s Third-Largest City Oct 27, 2026 In Yemen, Ansar Allah, known as the Houthis, used explosives to severely damage a critical road into Taiz, according to Human Rights Watch. The Hayjat al-Abd road is critical for delivering food, medicine and fuel to the city. Taiz has been besieged since fighting escalated between the Saudi-backed government and Ansar Allah. Fuel shortages in Taiz are straining hospitals, with one hospital forced to cut the number of ​incubators, putting newborn babies at risk. This is a neonatal nurse at the Yemeni-Swedish Hospital. > Nada Ahmed: “We reduced the numbers to 10 incubators because of the fuel shortage. There’s no oxygen. There’s no fuel to run the incubators, to keep the babies warm. We also moved from upstairs to downstairs for the babies’ safety. There is shelling near the hospital.” ## Seven Are Killed as Jordan Bombs Syria Following Deadly Church Attack Oct 27, 2026 In Syria, officials say seven people were killed, including women, children and an elderly man, after Jordan’s military struck sites in Daraa and Suwayda provinces. Jordan’s military said its fighter jets had killed and wounded “several terrorists,” without elaborating. The strikes followed a shooting at a Greek Orthodox church in Jordan on Friday that left nine people dead and 34 injured. Earlier on Monday, Jordan’s government said it had arrested three suspects behind the deadly church ​attack. ## Health Worker Killed in DRC as Ebola Cases Approach 10,000 Oct 27, 2026 In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, youths wielding machetes attacked two community health workers who were raising awareness of the Ebola outbreak in the country, killing one and wounding another. A local official said health workers in the area where the latest attack took place are sheltering at ​the general hospital under ⁠police guard. This is a U.N. spokesperson on the latest. > Daniela Gross de Almeida: “These incidents highlight how violence and mistrust can undermine the Ebola response and limit access to essential health services, as the numbers of confirmed cases approach 10,000, according to national authorities.” ## Russia and Ukraine Trade Drone Attacks Despite Local Ceasefire in Russian-Occupied Oleshky Oct 27, 2026 In Ukraine, a local ceasefire is underway in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, where fighting has left residents cut off from food and medical aid. The rare ceasefire to allow humanitarian access was brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump. Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine continue to trade attacks elsewhere. Overnight, Russia launched hundreds of drones and ballistic missiles across Ukraine, killing at least one person and injuring 15 others in the capital Kyiv, including students in a dormitory. And Russian officials said a Ukrainian drone killed a man and wounded six people in the western Russian city of Bryansk near Ukraine’s border, while another person was killed and 30 injured when a drone hit a bus in Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia. Meanwhile, a new report submitted to the U.N. General Assembly finds Russian officials committed war crimes by directing attacks against civilian targets in Ukraine, as well as crimes against humanity through continuous attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. This is Pablo de Greiff, a member of the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine. > Pablo de Greiff: “Those attacks that target civilian objects indispensable to the civilian population are unlawful and amount to war crimes.”

items.title: National and International News in Focus: Oct. 27 | National | wktv.com
items.excerpt: ## Voters in Israel are deciding whether to oust Netanyahu after 3 years of war JERUSALEM (AP) — Israelis are voting in a pivotal election as the country grapples with unfinished wars and divisions over its future. There is high turnout. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu voted just after midday. He faces a strong challenge from former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. Polls show neither candidate's party is likely to gain enough support for a parliamentary majority, leading to possibly weeks of negotiations over forming a winning coalition. The election is Israel's first national vote since the Oct. 7 attacks and serves as a referendum on Netanyahu's leadership. The outcome could shape Israel's identity as either more nationalist and religious or liberal democratic. ... ## Localized ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump starts as Nordic leaders speak to Putin and Zelenskyy MYKOLAIV, ... first lady Melania Trump, aims to allow the delivery of aid later this week to the city of Oleshky, where supplies have run dangerously low. Despite the ceasefire, Russia continues missile attacks on other cities. Meanwhile, Finland’s president and Norway’s prime minister spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin and later with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The Nordic leaders described their talks with Putin as “frank and substantive.” The Oleshky ceasefire is expected to last through Saturday, but its success remains uncertain. ... ## Congo’s Ebola outbreak tops 10,000 cases as authorities race to slow the spread in African countries BUNIA, Congo (AP) — Congo’s fast-moving Ebola outbreak has topped 10,000 confirmed cases as authorities race to slow the spread across Africa. Data from Congo's Ministry of Health on Tuesday showed there have been a total of 10,060 confirmed cases, nearly half of whom have died. It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history and was declared in May. It is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Response teams are battling armed conflict, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation. It has spread farther across Africa than any previous Ebola outbreak, reaching three regions with cases recorded in Kenya and Nigeria as well. ## Risks spelled out for Anthropic investors include blowback from runaway AI Any time a company looks to start selling shares on Wall Street, it’s required to disclose potential risks for investors. In the case of artificial intelligence giant Anthropic, that has included the possibility that its products could threaten nothing less than humanity itself. The risks laid out by the San Francisco company in its filing Monday with the Securities and Exchange Commission range from the mundane to involvement in cyberattacks and the spread of dangerous misinformation. In selling itself to investors, Anthropic presents its own initial public offering as a step toward mitigating the risks it believes AI poses.

items.title: Federal Reserve rate hikes are coming, but not this week: CNBC survey
items.excerpt: Published Tue, Oct 27 2026 7:10 AM EDT Updated 2 Hours Ago ... The Federal Reserve has considerable work to do. But it's not going to do it in October. That's the key finding in CNBC's latest Fed Survey of 30 fund managers, strategists and economists, which showed that 93% expect a pause at the Fed meeting taking place this week and 76% anticipate a rate hike at its next meeting in December. And more than half say the Fed will hike next year by an average of about two rate hikes. "Their hesitancy to raise rates is unfathomable after an extended period of monetary and fiscal generosity, with nominal GDP running 6-8%, and when the leading indicators of inflation are uniformly warm to hot,'' said Richard Bernstein, global head of macro investing at Janus Henderson Investors. A plurality of 40% say the Fed must slow growth below potential to solve the inflation problem. That compares with 27% who say the Fed does not need to slow the economy and 23% who say the Fed has to slow the economy only somewhat. The survey, which CNBC conducts before every Fed meeting, found that 70% see the inflation problem as broader than just the rising price of energy. The U.S. crude oil benchmark is forecast to be at $88 a barrel six months from now, up from $82 in the September survey, but below the current level of $101. Asked what the Fed should do at the current meeting, 30% said it should hike rates now. At least two Fed voters are expected by survey respondents to dissent from the decision to keep rates unchanged. "The aggregate demand data (probably north of 7%...) and the inflation data point to the strong need to hike rates,'' wrote John Ryding, chief economic advisor for Brean Capital, LLC. Not all agree. Some are concerned with a weakening economy. "The Iran War is intensifying, real wages are falling, interest rates are rising, and the AI-fueled stock market looks shaky," wrote Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics. "Inflation is high, but there's little sign it is becoming entrenched. This isn't the time for more Fed rate hikes. Amid numerous shocks and challenges — including high inflation, expected Fed rate hikes and a continuation of high oil prices — respondents still see economic growth remaining above potential, or the level of growth that doesn't lead to inflation or deflation. Forecasts of GDP for this year rose to 2.4%. They ticked down slightly since the last survey but still hover above potential at 2.2% for 2027. Growth in 2025 came in at 2.05%. Respondents in aggregate put the risk of the U.S. entering a recession in the next year at 26%, down from 29% in the last survey. ... Unemployment is forecast to remain steady at 4.2% through the remainder of the year but rise to 4.4% in 2027. The Consumer Price Index is seen ticking down to 3.6% from the current pace of 3.7% in September but fall meaningfully next year to 2.6%.

items.excerpt: Treasury yields moved higher on Tuesday as the Federal Reserve's two-day monetary policy meeting kicked off and investors digested a spate of economic data releases. The benchmark 10-year Treasury Add To Watchlist yield rose more than 1 basis point to 5.003%, as did the 30-year Treasury Add To Watchlist bond to 5.316%. The 2-year Treasury Add To Watchlist note yield was up 3 basis points at 4.741%. One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions. The Fed was set to begin its two-day monetary policy meeting on Tuesday, with the central bank's latest interest rate decision due on Wednesday. Traders are widely expecting policymakers to keep the interest rate unchanged at the current target range of 3.75% to ... Those on Wall Street on Tuesday assessed the latest reading on durable goods orders, which increased 1.8% in September. That was slightly above the 1.7% rise that economists polled by Dow Jones expected. Traders also reacted to fresh data on consumer confidence and new home sales. In September, new home sales stood at 676,000, marking a 0.6% fall from August but coming in above the 653,000 Dow Jones consensus estimate. Meanwhile, consumer confidence in October rose to 91.7, beating the 81.0 that was estimated. The latest publication of the personal consumption expenditures index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, is due on Thursday.

items.title: Democrats still poised to make gains, but poll shows ...
items.excerpt: Democrats retain significant midterm electoral advantages, with key data pointing to them being the favorites to win control of the U.S. House. But, there are indications of why a potential wave could be limited, a new NPR/PBS News/Marist poll finds. The poll also sheds light on the issues driving voters across the ideological spectrum. The cost of living continues to be top of mind overall with a third of people saying they've experienced financial hardship in the past year and 4 in 10 saying their personal finances have gotten worse. "The economy is at the top of my list right now," said Shun Maurice, a 47-year-old from Arizona who participated in the poll. He's an independent who leans toward Democrats and said high food and gas prices are a strain. "They're too expensive for everybody, no matter who you voted for," he said. "They're just too expensive for the American people in general, and I don't like that." Preserving democracy also continues to resonate with Democrats and independents, while immigration is the biggest concern for self-described MAGA supporters. The poll of 1,289 registered voters was conducted Oct. 19-20. When registered voters are mentioned, the margin of error is +/- 3.7 percentage points. When likely voters are mentioned, it is +/- 3.8 points. ### Most don't think Trump is doing a good job and don't like him This was the first survey this cycle that Marist applied a likely voter screen, and on multiple questions, likely voters were — within the margin of error — slightly less likely than registered voters to disapprove of the president. Likely voters overall were also slightly less likely to want Democrats to run Congress. Likely voters are something of a special sauce in polling. Survey researchers apply various metrics — like levels of enthusiasm, past voting history and how important voting is to different respondents — to try to identify the subsample of people who are most likely to vote. ### Trump leans into unprecedented power ahead of midterm elections In this survey, just 38% of registered voters approved of the job President Trump is doing, with 61% disapproving (-23). Likely voters gave him a 40% to 59% rating (-19), still not very good, but even a slight margin can make a difference in how significant the gains either party might make in the election are. That said, an equal share — 53% — of registered and likely voters said they "strongly disapprove" of the job Trump is doing, tied with last month as the highest ever in the poll. Trump's favorability rating is even lower — just 37% of likely voters have a favorable impression of Trump, while 59% have a negative one. ### Democrats retain the edge on the congressional ballot Democrats also had a strong advantage on which party's candidate people said they are more likely to vote for in their district if the election were held today, known as the generic congressional ballot. Among registered voters, it was a 10-point advantage. With likely voters, it was 8 points, still indicative of Democratic gains. When Democrats have had that kind of lead on the congressional ballot, they have historically done very well. On average, it was +7 in 2018 and +12 in 2006. In both years, Democrats won the House with at least 30 seats flipped. But that was before the 2020 Census and ensuing regular redistricting — and the rare, mid-decade redistricting in the last year and a half after Trump asked Republican states to redraw their maps to potentially give Republicans more seats. Though Democrats followed suit, both redistricting periods have tilted congressional seats in Republicans' direction and given them a relative advantage nationally. Perhaps because of some of those structural disadvantages and past performance, there is a notable degree of nervousness among Democrats. While 98% of Democratic likely voters said they would vote for a Democrat, just 81% thought the Democrat would win, a 17-point difference. Republicans were only 10 points less likely to believe their candidate would win. Notably, among independents, a higher share thought the Democratic candidate would win. ... ### Democrats also have the enthusiasm advantage, but there are some caution flags, too Democratic likely voters are 10 points more likely to say they are "very enthusiastic" about voting (71% vs. 61%). That's actually wider than the difference between Democratic and Republican registered voters in the poll. The caution for Democrats, though, is that several of their key pillar groups are not very enthusiastic to vote, and Republicans have closed the gap on who is following the election "very closely." Just 42% of likely voters under 45, 53% of non-white voters and 56% of white women with college degrees said they are "very enthusiastic" to vote. All of those groups disapproved of the job Trump is doing. Compare that to pro-Trump groups — MAGA voters (68%), white women without degrees (66%) and white evangelical voters (61%). For independents, 48% report being very enthusiastic to vote. Traditionally, younger, as well as Black and Latino voters turn out at disproportionately lower rates in midterm elections. But with the realignment under Trump, more white, college-educated voters are voting Democratic and, as a group, they turn out at the highest rates. When it comes to paying close attention, last month just 34% of registered Republicans said they're following the election very closely, compared to 42% of Democrats. Now, they're even – 46% of Democrats and 45% of Republicans said they're paying very close attention. When it comes to likely voters, there's no difference either – 51% of Democrats to 50% of Republicans. On the positive side for ... Three-quarters of likely voters are confident that their state and local governments will run a fair and accurate election. That includes solid majorities of Democrats (88%), Republicans (68%) and independents (75%), but Republicans were 20 points less likely than Democrats to think they would be run well. MAGA supporters were almost 30 points less likely.

items.excerpt: # AP Entertainment SummaryBrief at 9:37 a.m. EDT - AP - Oct 27, 2026 - Oct 27, 2026 Updated 39 mins ago Taylor Swift, Lyle Lovett and more inducted into Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Taylor Swift has been inducted into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame, alongside Lyle Lovett, Shawn Camp, Lee Thomas Miller, Bruce Channel and J.I. Allison. Swift signed her first publishing deal in Nashville at the age of 14. She returned to the city on Monday during the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame annual gala celebration. She said it was an incredible honor to be inducted and described soaking up the lessons from other writers like a sponge. Also honored was country music icon George Strait with the organization's Career Maker Award. He said the songwriters helped to make his career. Jay-Z picks himself to headline the Super Bowl halftime show at SoFi Stadium in Southern California LOS ANGELES (AP) — Jay-Z will headline the Super Bowl halftime show on February 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California. The NFL, Apple Music, and Roc Nation announced the news Monday night. NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said he always wanted Jay-Z to perform when the time felt right. Jay-Z expressed excitement about the opportunity, calling it a dream come true. His Roc Nation has partnered with the NFL since 2019 to produce entertainment presentations, including the halftime show. Jay-Z, who has won 25 Grammy Awards, will perform at the stadium where he recently celebrated the 30th anniversary of his debut album, “Reasonable Doubt.” Andrea Bocelli concerts in Indonesia to proceed despite opposition from Muslim clerics JAKARTA, Indonesia (AP) — Italian tenor Andrea Bocelli's concerts in Indonesia will proceed despite opposition from the country's top Muslim clerical body. The Indonesian Ulema Council demanded the cancellation due to Bocelli's past support for Israel. Indonesia, a strong supporter of Palestinians, does not have formal diplomatic relations with Israel. The concerts are scheduled for October 31 at Borobudur Temple and November 3 in Jakarta. Promoter Shoemaker Live insists the events will support Indonesia's tourism and culture sectors. Bocelli plans to dedicate songs to humanity and world peace. The council argues the concerts could hurt Indonesians who support Palestinians. After pushback, the Dutch reverse course and withdraw from Eurovision again AMSTERDAM (AP) — The Netherlands is withdrawing from participating in the Eurovision Song Contest, reversing a decision in September to return to the show. NPO, the umbrella organization for public broadcasters in the country announced in September it would send a performer to the event, after a subsidiary had said a month earlier it would boycott the contest for a second year. Earlier this month, hundreds of NPO employees sent a letter opposing Dutch participation. A number of prominent Dutch media personalities also publicly objected to the move. Japanese manga artist Tetsuya Chiba, known for his boxing masterpiece 'Ashita no Joe,' dies at 87 TOKYO (AP) — Tetsuya Chiba, a legendary Japanese manga artist best known for his boxing series “Ashita no Joe,” or “Fighting for Tomorrow,” has died. He was 87. Chiba’s masterpiece “Ashita no Joe” series, depicting an aspiring young generation during Japan’s postwar era, became a national sensation. The series was so popular that fans even attended a mock funeral for the protagonist’s rival. Chiba was also a vocal supporter of peace and freedom of expression, telling stories of his harrowing memories of war as a child in his autobiographical stories and manga. Chiba’s publisher, Kodansha Ltd., said Tuesday that the artist died at a Tokyo hospital last Thursday. Music Review: Nickelback is in familiar form on cameo-heavy 'Everything Under the Sun' Nickelback’s 11th studio album “Everything Under the Sun” is a mix of hard-rock anthems, radio-friendly hits, and emotional ballads with a few surprises. The Canadian rockers mostly stick to their successful formula, which has been both criticized and celebrated for over 30 years. The Associated Press' Dennis Waszak Jr. says in his review that the album out Friday is a showcase of everything Nickelback does best. Highlights on the 12-track album include the high-energy “Rattle The Cage” and rock ballads “I Already Know” and “Make Me Love You.” Guest appearances include Sammy Hagar and actor Ryan Reynolds. But those looking for more than their formula may not enjoy it. Walter Koenig, Ensign Chekov on the original 'Star Trek' series, dies at 90 LOS ANGELES (AP) — Actor Walter Koenig, known for playing Ensign Pavel Chekov on “Star Trek,” has died at 90. His talent agent confirmed he passed away Monday at his home in Los Angeles. Koenig's role as Chekov showcased a future where rival nations worked together. “Star Trek” aired from 1966 to 1969 and gained a massive fan following. Koenig's castmate George Takei praised him as a writer, teacher, and friend. Koenig appeared in seven “Star Trek” movies and wrote a book about the series. He also acted in “Babylon 5” and ventured into computer games. Pioneering industrial band Ministry is done. Take it from founder Al Jourgensen: 'It's time to go' NEW YORK (AP) — Ministry, the pioneering industrial rock band that paved the way for acts like Nine Inch Nails, is calling it quits after 45 years. Founder Al Jourgensen confirms the band is done after releasing their 17th album, “Hate To Go — Take Out Or Delivery,” on Oct. 30. A farewell tour will follow. Jourgensen told The Associated Press he believes it's time for a new generation to take over. The final album reflects their multidecade run without leaning into nostalgia and utilizes artificial intelligence in unsettling and surprising ways. Jourgensen jokes about retiring to herd goats and denies wanting a lasting legacy. “We did what we could,” he says of his band. Chris Brown avoids prison time for brawling at a London nightclub LONDON (AP) — Chris Brown has avoided prison time for beating a music producer with a tequila bottle at a London nightclub three years ago. On Monday, a court gave him an eight-month sentence, suspended for a year. Brown, 37, faced up to three years in prison after pleading guilty to affray in July. The incident occurred at Tape, a private club in Mayfair, in February 2023. Affray involves unlawful violence that causes fear for safety. Brown's plea deal led prosecutors to drop more serious charges. He was arrested in May 2025 after returning to the UK for a concert. What to Stream: 'Minions & Monsters,' Matthew Perry, Daddy Yankee and 'The Gilded Age' A new docuseries about Matthew Perry and the latest Minions movie are among the new streaming releases this week. The Minions return in “Minions & Monsters,” where they become silent movie stars in the 1920s. On Paramount+, “Hanging by a Wire” chronicles a dramatic 2023 rescue in Pakistan. Daddy Yankee releases a new album, “La Postal,” exploring themes of love. Nickelback and Dustin Lynch also have new albums out. On Netflix, a docuseries on Matthew Perry premieres Tuesday. “The Gilded Age” returns for its fourth season on HBO Max. Plus, the video game “Phantom Blade Zero” debuts Thursday.
